blocks.content: A zombie process is one of the most frequently misunderstood terms in all of Unix and Linux, largely because the name suggests something has gone badly wrong when, in the vast majority of cases, it is a brief, completely normal, and even necessary part of how a parent process learns how its child actually finished.

This chapter builds directly on the fork chapter parent child relationship, explaining exactly what a zombie is, why the kernel deliberately keeps one around instead of cleaning up immediately, and when zombies actually become a real problem worth worrying about.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197909-919924085.png
1. What a Zombie Process Actually Is
blocks.text: 1. What a Zombie Process Actually Is

blocks.content: When a process finishes running, whether by returning from main or calling exit directly, the kernel does not immediately erase every trace of it. Almost all of its resources really are freed right away, its memory, its open file descriptors, everything genuinely expensive. But one small thing is deliberately kept behind: an entry in the process table holding its process ID, its exit status, and a handful of accounting fields.

A process sitting in exactly this state, finished but with this minimal entry still present, is called a zombie. It is not running, it is not consuming any real memory or CPU time, it is essentially just a placeholder record, waiting for something specific to happen before it can be fully erased.
2. Why the Kernel Deliberately Keeps This Entry Around
blocks.text: 2. Why the Kernel Deliberately Keeps This Entry Around

blocks.content: The reason is entirely about communication between parent and child. A parent process very often needs to know how its child actually finished, whether it exited successfully, exited with an error code, or was killed by a signal, and it typically does not learn this until sometime after the child has already terminated.

If the kernel erased every trace of the child the instant it finished, that exit status would simply be lost, with no way for the parent to ever retrieve it. Keeping a minimal zombie entry around is the deliberate mechanism that preserves this one piece of information until the parent actually asks for it.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197910-539513157.png
blocks.alt: Why the Kernel Deliberately Keeps This Entry Around

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A zombie is a finished child process whose exit status the kernel is holding onto, because its parent has not yet collected it.
3. The Zombie Lifecycle

The full lifecycle is short and completely deterministic. A process runs normally, terminates by calling exit, becomes a zombie the instant it terminates, and stays a zombie right up until its parent calls wait or waitpid, at which point the kernel hands the exit status to the parent and fully removes the zombie entry from the process table.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197910-578738446.png
The parent side: wait and waitpid
blocks.text: The parent side: wait and waitpid

blocks.content: Calling wait from a parent process blocks that parent until at least one of its children becomes a zombie, at which point it immediately collects that child exit status and removes its zombie entry. If a zombie child already exists at the moment wait is called, it returns immediately with no blocking at all, exactly the pattern the fork chapter shell example relied on.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197910-99075678.png
blocks.alt: The parent side: wait and waitpid

blocks.content: 4. When Zombies Actually Become a Problem
blocks.text: 4. When Zombies Actually Become a Problem

blocks.content: A zombie that exists for a brief moment, right up until its parent calls wait, is completely normal and harmless. The real problem shows up specifically when a parent process is poorly written and simply never calls wait or waitpid at all, even though its children keep finishing.

Every child that finishes under a parent like this becomes a zombie that never gets collected, and stays a zombie indefinitely, permanently occupying an entry in the process table. Do this repeatedly, spawning many children that a broken parent never reaps, and the accumulated zombie entries can meaningfully consume table space and add real pressure on the available process ID range.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409296224-303955352.png
blocks.alt: When Zombies Actually Become a Problem

blocks.content: Spotting them with ps

Zombie processes are easy to spot with standard process listing tools. A process shown with state Z, or with defunct appended to its command name, is a zombie sitting in exactly this uncollected state.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409296226-830971444.png
5. Why You Cannot Simply Kill a Zombie
blocks.text: 5. Why You Cannot Simply Kill a Zombie

blocks.content: A very common instinct when someone first sees a zombie in a process listing is to try killing it directly, expecting that to clean it up. This does not work, and understanding why reinforces exactly what a zombie actually is: it is not a running process at all, it has already terminated, there is no active program left to receive or respond to a kill signal.

The only two things that actually resolve a zombie are the parent calling wait or waitpid to collect it, or the parent itself terminating, at which point the zombie gets reparented, forward pointer to the sibling orphan processes chapter, typically up to a dedicated system process that reaps it automatically.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409296226-565617685.png
blocks.alt: Why You Cannot Simply Kill a Zombie

blocks.content: 6. Writing a Parent That Reaps Its Children Properly
blocks.text: 6. Writing a Parent That Reaps Its Children Properly

blocks.content: A well written parent process that spawns children avoids zombie buildup entirely by handling the SIGCHLD signal, which the kernel automatically sends to a parent every time one of its children terminates. A signal handler for SIGCHLD typically calls waitpid in a loop, collecting every child that has finished, promptly and automatically, with no manual polling required.

8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming a zombie process is consuming meaningful CPU or memory, when in reality it holds only a minimal process table entry, essentially just an exit status waiting to be collected.","Trying to kill a zombie directly with a signal, when a zombie is not an active process at all and cannot receive or respond to signals.","Assuming every zombie indicates a bug, when a zombie existing briefly between a child terminating and its parent calling wait is the completely normal, expected mechanism, not a failure."]
items: Assuming a zombie process is consuming meaningful CPU or memory, when in reality it holds only a minimal process table entry, essentially just an exit status waiting to be collected.
Trying to kill a zombie directly with a signal, when a zombie is not an active process at all and cannot receive or respond to signals.
Assuming every zombie indicates a bug, when a zombie existing briefly between a child terminating and its parent calling wait is the completely normal, expected mechanism, not a failure.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain precisely why zombies exist, the kernel needs somewhere to hold a finished child exit status until the parent collects it, and to describe the correct fix for zombie accumulation: the parent handling SIGCHLD and calling waitpid in a loop, rather than the common wrong answer of trying to kill the zombie directly.
Zombies are what happens when a parent has not yet collected a finished child. The next chapter covers the reverse situation entirely: what happens to a child when its parent disappears first.
